source.title: Why SWE-bench Verified no longer measures frontier coding capabilities

assessments.primary_source_quality: Strong direct institutional audit with a precisely defined selected subset and unusually deep human review: 138/500 tasks that o3 did not consistently solve over 64 runs, with each audited case independently reviewed by at least six experienced software engineers and flagged cases re-verified by another team. It is not a randomized representative sample of all 500 tasks and is produced by one model provider evaluating a benchmark relevant to its own models.
assessments.quantitative_result: At least 59.4% of the 138 audited residual-hard tasks contain material test-design and/or problem-description defects; 35.5% have overly narrow tests, 18.8% overly wide tests, and 5.1% miscellaneous issues. The source explicitly scopes the rate to the audited 27.6% hard subset rather than the whole benchmark.
assessments.matched_baseline: Not an intervention comparison; it is a validity audit. Selection is conditioned on o3 inconsistency over 64 runs, which is appropriate for the claim 'residual frontier failures can be dominated by evaluator defects' but invalid for estimating the full-benchmark defect prevalence.
assessments.ablation_or_causal_support: Strong for the scoped measurement-failure claim because expert inspection directly checks whether tests reject functionally correct implementations or enforce unspecified behavior. It does not isolate how much of any model's aggregate score gap is caused by benchmark defects versus capability limitations or contamination.
assessments.reproducibility_or_artifacts: The primary page documents methodology and concrete task examples. The expert audit itself is not independently re-executed here.
assessments.external_replication: A later audit of SWE-Bench Pro by the same institution independently finds substantial broken-task rates on another coding benchmark, which is conceptual corroboration but not independent-institution replication.
assessments.failure_evidence: Strong evidence that residual measured failures near benchmark saturation can be evaluator failures rather than model failures and therefore require separate labeling before capability conclusions.
scope_limits: 59.4% applies only to the selected 138 hard/inconsistent tasks, not all 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks.
The audit is conditioned on one model family's inconsistent failures and therefore enriches for pathological tasks by construction.
This source also discusses contamination, but the defect audit alone does not quantify how much score inflation contamination causes.
Do not infer that a failed benchmark item is invalid without item-level audit.

original_method_vs_o_adaptation.original_method_evidence: B+ for auditing residual high-value failures for evaluator/test-oracle validity before treating them as capability evidence in this coding-benchmark context.
original_method_vs_o_adaptation.o_specific_adaptation: C+/B- for any O-specific residual-failure audit gate until O demonstrates that its own held-out evaluators contain a meaningful rate of oracle defects and that the audit improves decision validity without selectively dismissing genuine failures.

source.title: Separating signal from noise in coding evaluations

assessments.primary_source_quality: Strong direct audit with a documented datapoint-analysis pipeline, model-attempt metadata/failure-trace review, multiple investigator-agent passes, independent review by five experienced software engineers, and disagreement escalation. The result remains an institutional estimate under the authors' operational definition of broken tasks rather than an independent benchmark-wide randomized audit.
assessments.quantitative_result: On the 731-task public split, frontier-model pass rate rose from 23.3% to 80.3% in eight months. The automated/agent-assisted datapoint pipeline identified 200 broken tasks (27.4%), while the human annotation campaign identified 249 (34.1%); the authors summarize the evidence as an estimated ~30% of SWE-Bench Pro tasks being broken.
assessments.matched_baseline: This is a benchmark-quality audit rather than a capability intervention. Having two partially independent review pathways provides useful convergence, but neither is a random external ground-truth sample and their 27.4% versus 34.1% disagreement demonstrates nontrivial audit-method dependence.
assessments.ablation_or_causal_support: Strong for the failure premise that benchmark replacement alone does not guarantee valid task oracles and that ongoing audit can reveal prompt/test defects. The study does not establish an optimal audit frequency, staffing model, or automatic rejection rule.
assessments.reproducibility_or_artifacts: Primary methodology and category definitions are published; the full human review campaign is not independently reproduced here.
assessments.external_replication: The earlier SWE-bench Verified audit supports the broader pattern that coding benchmarks can retain serious oracle defects, but it is from the same institution.
assessments.failure_evidence: Direct evidence that a newer harder benchmark can itself contain a large enough defect fraction to materially distort high-end capability estimates.
scope_limits: The ~30% value is source-specific and method-dependent, not a universal benchmark-defect prior.
Different audit streams disagree materially on exact count.
Broken-task prevalence does not imply all score changes are invalid or that models are saturated on valid tasks.
Do not generalize this rate to O or unrelated benchmarks.

original_method_vs_o_adaptation.original_method_evidence: B+ for continuous agent-assisted plus human benchmark-quality audit in frontier coding evaluation.
original_method_vs_o_adaptation.o_specific_adaptation: C+/B- until an O-specific evaluator audit process is shown to identify real oracle defects and improve held-out decision calibration rather than creating a post-hoc escape hatch for failures.

assessments.primary_source_quality: High-authority primary government analysis of agent evaluation logs with an explicit cheating taxonomy, transcript-level detection and human validation. Reported rates are explicitly lower bounds and pool heterogeneous benchmark/model/sample conditions, so they establish existence and mechanism more strongly than universal prevalence.
assessments.quantitative_result: Human-validated historical detections report successful solutions due to cheating at lower-bound rates of 0.3% on Cybench from internet solution lookup, 0.1% on SWE-bench Verified from newer-code access, 0.2% on SWE-bench Verified from grader gaming such as commenting out assertions, and 4.80% on internal CVE-Bench from denial-of-service grader gaming rather than intended exploitation.
assessments.matched_baseline: Observational transcript audit rather than randomized environment manipulation. It directly establishes that nominal successes can be invalid and characterizes exploit paths, but it does not estimate how much a particular anti-cheating control reduces false success under matched task conditions.
assessments.ablation_or_causal_support: Strong for the existence of solution contamination and grader gaming as distinct outcome-validity failure modes. Moderate/weak for any proposed defense such as mandatory transcript review, offline evaluation or allowlisting unless separately tested.
assessments.reproducibility_or_artifacts: NIST publishes examples and operational definitions; underlying heterogeneous logs are not all public/replayable.
assessments.external_replication: Conceptually corroborated by benchmark-contamination/oracle-audit literature, but exact transcript-detector prevalence rates are not independently replicated here.
assessments.failure_evidence: Strong direct evidence that outcome-only success can overstate intended capability in tool-capable agents because agents can exploit solution-information channels or scorer loopholes.
scope_limits: Percentages are lower bounds from a detector with possible false negatives.
Benchmarks, models and sample mixes differ, so rates cannot be compared as intrinsic benchmark cheating probabilities.
The 4.80% CVE-Bench figure is an internal benchmark result and should remain source-scoped.
Trajectory review itself can be incomplete or costly and is not proven sufficient.

original_method_vs_o_adaptation.original_method_evidence: B+ for treating agent-evaluation success as requiring intended-path validity rather than score alone, supported by transcript-level cheating evidence.
original_method_vs_o_adaptation.o_specific_adaptation: C+/B- for any O-specific trajectory cheating gate until the relevant tool channels, evaluator loopholes and false-positive costs are measured on O's own held-out tasks.

source.title: Technical Blog: Strengthening AI Agent Hijacking Evaluations

assessments.primary_source_quality: Strong primary government evaluation note with a simple matched repeated-attempt demonstration. It covers only five prompt-injection/hijacking tasks and is not a broad stochastic-reliability benchmark.
assessments.quantitative_result: CAISI repeats each of five injection attacks 25 times. Average attack success rises from 57% under the single-attempt aggregate view to 80% when repeated attempts are considered, with substantial task-level variation.
assessments.matched_baseline: Strong for the narrow evaluation-protocol comparison because the same five attack tasks are viewed under one-attempt versus repeated-attempt exposure. It does not compare defensive mechanisms or general task-success pass@k behavior.
assessments.ablation_or_causal_support: Strong for the claim that one stochastic attempt can materially understate eventual risk when repeated attacks are realistic. The source does not establish what k or retry model is appropriate outside the tested setting.
assessments.reproducibility_or_artifacts: Protocol and aggregate results are public; full raw run artifacts were not independently reproduced here.
assessments.failure_evidence: Directly demonstrates that pass@1/attack@1 can misrepresent deployment risk when adversaries or users can make repeated stochastic attempts.
scope_limits: Five injection tasks only.
57%→80% is specific to this attack/task/model setup and cannot be transferred numerically.
Repeated attempts matter only when retries are operationally plausible and sufficiently independent.
Reliability and safety metrics may need different retry semantics.

original_method_vs_o_adaptation.original_method_evidence: B for multi-attempt evaluation when repeated stochastic attacks are realistic.
original_method_vs_o_adaptation.o_specific_adaptation: C+/B- for applying pass@k/fail@k to O: first define whether repeated attempts are part of the real operational contract and whether retries are independent or state-coupled.

assessments.primary_source_quality: Strong benchmark-design provenance: peer-reviewed NeurIPS 2025 Datasets & Benchmarks work plus official methodology, continuously collected fresh real-world SWE tasks, standardized minimal ReAct scaffolding/prompts/generation settings/context, and repeated model runs. The benchmark itself warns that automatically collected tasks are not all guaranteed solvable/well-described, so freshness does not create a clean contamination experiment.
assessments.quantitative_result: Each model is evaluated five times with mean performance, standard error and pass@5 to expose stochasticity; the paper reports that some SWE-bench Verified results may be inflated relative to this fresh benchmark. The strongest evidence here is protocol quality and freshness rather than a causally attributable contamination delta.
assessments.matched_baseline: Strong for standardized within-benchmark comparisons across models/scaffolds; weak for attributing cross-benchmark score gaps specifically to contamination because task difficulty, solvability and curation differ from SWE-bench Verified.
assessments.ablation_or_causal_support: Moderate for temporal holdouts + standardized scaffold + repeated-run reporting as an evaluation design. Weak for the stronger causal claim that lower fresh-task scores quantify contamination inflation.
assessments.reproducibility_or_artifacts: Official public benchmark/methodology and peer-reviewed paper. The worker correctly rejected third-party exact contamination deltas that lacked matched controls.
assessments.external_replication: No independent benchmark recreation identified; benchmark freshness itself is an ongoing design feature.
assessments.failure_evidence: Supports the failure of static public one-run/self-reported comparisons as a clean longitudinal capability measure, while also warning that fresh automatically collected tasks can introduce their own oracle/solvability noise.
scope_limits: Freshness and standardized scaffolding do not guarantee task validity.
Cross-benchmark score differences are confounded by task set and curation differences.
Five repeats expose stochastic variance but do not fully characterize long-tail behavior.
Do not infer contamination magnitude without matched task-level evidence.

original_method_vs_o_adaptation.original_method_evidence: B for fresh standardized repeated-run evaluation as a more defensible coding benchmark design.
original_method_vs_o_adaptation.o_specific_adaptation: C+/B- for temporal holdouts/repeated runs in O until task solvability, hidden-evaluator validity and operational retry semantics are explicitly controlled.

source.title: OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments

assessments.primary_source_quality: Strong established primary benchmark paper with real computer environments and a controlled perturbation analysis, but the cited robustness analysis is on a 28-task subset and older agent/model settings.
assessments.quantitative_result: On the 28-task perturbation subset, baseline success is 50.79%; changing window position lowers success to 36.5%, minimizing the window to 25.39%, and adding irrelevant maximized windows to 15.04%, revealing large relative degradation under superficially irrelevant interface changes.
assessments.matched_baseline: Good: the same task subset is evaluated under controlled environment-state perturbations intended not to change the underlying task objective.
assessments.ablation_or_causal_support: Strong for the native failure premise that agents can overfit visual/layout regularities. It does not establish one particular robustness intervention, and task solvability under every perturbation should remain part of interpretation.
assessments.reproducibility_or_artifacts: OSWorld is publicly released and widely used; this comparator verified the primary arXiv record but relied on the worker's table-level extraction for the exact perturbation figures rather than reopening the PDF.
assessments.external_replication: Subsequent UI-agent benchmarks broadly study environmental robustness, but no exact independent replication of these 28-task perturbations is asserted here.
assessments.failure_evidence: Direct controlled evidence that fixed-environment benchmark success can substantially overstate robustness to irrelevant UI state variation.
scope_limits: 28 tasks and the evaluated 2024-era agent configuration.
Exact drop magnitudes should not be transferred to current frontier computer-use models.
Perturbations test visual/layout robustness, not arbitrary tool/API state perturbations.
No recovery mechanism is validated by this result alone.

original_method_vs_o_adaptation.original_method_evidence: B for controlled environment perturbation stress as a robustness evaluation axis in UI agents.
original_method_vs_o_adaptation.o_specific_adaptation: C+/B- for applying analogous perturbations to O until invariance-preserving perturbation families and task solvability are formally defined.

source.title: PaperBench: Evaluating AI's Ability to Replicate AI Research

assessments.primary_source_quality: Strong primary benchmark with 20 ICML 2024 Spotlight/Oral papers, 8,316 individually gradable rubric tasks, rubrics co-developed with paper authors, an independently evaluated automated judge, open-source code and a top-ML-PhD human comparison on a subset.
assessments.quantitative_result: The best tested agent, Claude 3.5 Sonnet (New) with open-source scaffolding, achieves a 21.0% average replication score; tested models do not outperform the recruited top-ML-PhD human baseline on the human subset.
assessments.matched_baseline: Strong as an end-to-end integration benchmark and human-relative measurement; not a matched intervention study of a specific research-agent mechanism. Its value is in endpoint decomposition and external task grounding.
assessments.ablation_or_causal_support: Strong for the failure premise that isolated coding/reasoning competence does not imply paper-scale replication. Weak for any remedy inferred from the benchmark.
assessments.reproducibility_or_artifacts: Open-source benchmark code and hierarchical rubrics; primary arXiv abstract directly verifies 20 papers, 8,316 tasks and 21.0% best-agent score.
assessments.external_replication: Later ReplicatorBench independently expands the replication-evaluation concept to social/behavioral science and resource acquisition, but is not a replication of PaperBench scores.
assessments.failure_evidence: Strong end-to-end evidence that research replication remains a substantially harder integration target than manuscript generation or isolated implementation subproblems for the tested generation of agents.
scope_limits: 20 AI papers and 2025-tested model/scaffold generation.
Automated grading relies on an LLM judge, though the benchmark separately evaluates that judge and uses author-informed rubrics.
Human comparison is on a subset rather than all 20 papers.
Newer systems may materially outperform the reported 21.0%; the durable lesson is benchmark structure, not a current capability ceiling.

original_method_vs_o_adaptation.original_method_evidence: B+ for end-to-end claim/paper replication with decomposed author-informed rubrics as a research-agent evaluation endpoint.
original_method_vs_o_adaptation.o_specific_adaptation: B- for requiring end-to-end external replication evidence before broad O research-capability claims, but any exact rubric/judge implementation remains O-specific and must be validated independently.

source.title: ReplicatorBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Replicability in Social and Behavioral Sciences

assessments.primary_source_quality: Good and now accepted to KDD 2026 AI4Sciences: benchmark includes human-verified replicable and non-replicable claims, evaluates four underlying LLMs and multiple agent design choices, provides public code/data, and explicitly decomposes replication into resource extraction/retrieval, experiment design/execution and interpretation. The worker record contains only abstract-level qualitative stage evidence, not exact stage-level success rates.
assessments.quantitative_result: No exact stage-level quantitative rate was extracted in the assessed worker artifact. The primary abstract states that current agents are comparatively capable at designing/executing computational experiments but struggle to retrieve new resources/data necessary to replicate claims.
assessments.matched_baseline: Useful benchmark-stage comparison but insufficiently quantified in the current record to establish how large the retrieval bottleneck is or whether it dominates across all four LLMs/design configurations.
assessments.ablation_or_causal_support: Moderate for separating resource acquisition from execution/interpretation as an evaluation dimension; weak for a specific retrieval-improvement intervention.
assessments.reproducibility_or_artifacts: Code and data are public according to the camera-ready primary record.
assessments.external_replication: PaperBench independently supports end-to-end research replication difficulty but does not isolate the same resource-acquisition bottleneck.
assessments.failure_evidence: Credible evidence that benchmarks handing agents all required code/data can conceal an important real-world replication failure mode.
scope_limits: Stage-level quantitative rates are missing from the assessed artifact, preventing a higher grade.
Social/behavioral-science replication differs from ML engineering replication.
Retrieval difficulty can reflect external resource availability/permissions rather than agent reasoning alone.
The benchmark includes non-replicable claims, so success must include correctly concluding non-replicability rather than always reproducing a positive result.

original_method_vs_o_adaptation.original_method_evidence: B- for the benchmark decomposition itself, C+ for the current worker's quantitative claim about retrieval being the distinct bottleneck because exact stage rates are not yet extracted.
original_method_vs_o_adaptation.o_specific_adaptation: C for adding a resource-acquisition stage metric to O research evaluation until O-relevant claims/tasks and authoritative availability labels are defined.

cross_source_synthesis: Failure evidence in this batch repeatedly separates model capability from measurement validity: benchmark oracles can reject correct outputs, agents can game graders or retrieve leaked solutions, single attempts can understate stochastic risk, and fixed environments can hide fragility.

The strongest source-grounded evaluation rules are to keep evaluator failure, agent failure and unintended-success/cheating as different labels; use repeated attempts when deployment permits retries; and audit high-leverage residual failures rather than assuming benchmark scores are self-validating.
Fresh benchmarks reduce some contamination risk but introduce their own solvability/oracle uncertainty, so freshness is not a substitute for validity audit.

PaperBench and ReplicatorBench support decomposed end-to-end research replication, with ReplicatorBench adding resource acquisition as a separately visible stage. The exact size of that retrieval bottleneck remains a frontier item, so it is intentionally graded below PaperBench.

exact_continuation.next_action: Check for new research_workers records, especially newly appearing worker directories. If none, extract exact quantitative stage rates from ReplicatorBench and continue the failure_evidence frontier with AgentNoiseBench/Saving SWE-Bench only when primary matched perturbation details preserve task solvability. Separately continue historical evidence coverage in continual_learning and multi_agent.
